label: paragraph_title

label: text
text: TAKING HIS FANCY.

label: text
text: When Admiral Dewey Visited the Colony.

label: text
text: There is in Hongkong, in the person of Mr. Berton Holmes, of education film fame, a chief amang us "takin' notes" which he will use for the illustration of his lectures.

label: text
text: The main object of Mr. Holmes's tour is to film the ruins at Angkor which were lately visited by His Excellency the Governor, but he is obtaining a little local colour during the break he has made in his journey here.

label: text
text: "I'm just taking what strikes my fancy," he told a "China Mail" representative who chatted with him in the lounge of the Hotel. "If a woman with a child strapped to her back or a ricsha coolie attracts me," I just take them because I know if they interest me they will interest the people at home. I have taken the bus discharging its passengers at Repulse Bay where I am staying," he added.

label: text
text: "No, it isn't likely that the people I take will feature in the Paramount Topical weekly film," said Mr. Holmes in reply to the query of the newspaper man who recalled that Mr. Holmes's name used to figure in most of the Paramount films. "I am entirely on my own now and use the material I obtain for the purpose of my lecture tours."

label: text
text: Mr. Holmes was for several years entirely responsible for the production of Paramount's weekly news film and it is only lately that he gave that up in favour of his own work. In the course of his hunts for film copy he came to Hongkong as early as 1899 and created a great deal of interest in that he was the first man to take a cinematograph film here. He was very proud of this achievement, particularly in that the film was very much in the nature of what is called in newspaper parlance a "scoop." He had received the "tip" that Admiral Dewey was returning after his victory over the Spaniards at Manila Bay to embark at Hongkong for Home where he would reap the glory and reward of his success. "I got him, too," remarked Mr. Holmes, with great satisfaction.

label: text
text: Since this historic occasion Mr. Holmes has called at Hongkong once or twice in the course of his travels in the undertaking of which he is actuated by the belief that there is a very large thinking public which finds in the films he is able to take what they are unable to enjoy themselves—“the satisfaction of the ‘instinct of travel which is set deeply in each one of us,” as he puts it.

label: text
text: From the name he has made for himself as an educational film expert it might be deduced that Mr. Holmes has set his face against films which have no educative value in themselves, but this would be a very wrong impression. Mr. Holmes thinks that most films serve a useful purpose in taking people out of their every day existence, and he has many friends among popular film "stars." "I had lunch with the King and Queen just before I came out," was a remark smilingly made which made the newspaper man open his eyes with surprise until Mr. Holmes qualified it with, "Oh, I mean at Hollywood, where I was the guest of Doug and Mary—we always call them that."

label: text
text: taken place in Hongkong since he was last here, Mr. Holmes, like many others, describes as "truly remarkable." Asked if there was anything else which particularly struck him Mr. Holmes unhesitatingly remarked "Yes, the price of drinks. I'm not exaggerating when I say that one pays no more for "run" liquor in the States than one has to here. The same applies to living generally. I used to feel ashamed to pay a scotland what was looked upon then as ample for carrying me also to pay what was charged for what we Americans call "eats." I shall go out with an easy conscience on that score now though.

label: text
text: Mr. Burton Holmes is a friend of Mr. Lowell Thomas, whose films of Allenby in Palestine created such a furore when shown in England. Mr. Holmes

label: paragraph_title

label: text
text:
too, has shown some of his films and lectured in England but he confesses that he finds himself more at home in America where he has no difficulty in getting together large audiences. This, it is not difficult to understand, for his is a personality which it is hard to withstand, as the "China Mail" man found when he looked at his watch and found how the time had flown. Mr. Holmes looks what he is—a traveller and a "looker on," with a bronzed, handsome face, rather tall figure, exceedingly well groomed, a trim "military" bearing, and roving eyes which seem everlastingly to be on the look out for material.

They preferred hats with height-giving crowns, with softening brims extending no further than the tip of a petite nose, and with gorgeous colourings. Others wore lettuce and lily-leaf shades which made the tennis stand resemble an animated garden.

label: text
text: Dresses, on the whole, were not inclined to be long, but their cut invariably set out graceful figures when the folds were fondled by the wind. Sleeves varied between the short and the no sleeve at all. A few of the ladies carried Japanese sunshades or dainty parasols which when opened added to the kaleidoscopic effect and, from a more practical point of view, served as a compromise between accepting or refusing Sir James Cantlie's advice.

label: text
text:
But this is entirely apart from the subject: Miss Laura A. Holden, manager in Shanghai for a Paris firm, has emphatically declared that Paris will have to look to Shanghai for the latest in feminine modes and that styles in Shanghai are two years ahead of gay Paree in daring and everything else! She claims that the bobbed-hair craze started in the Model Settlement and that when she arrived there two years ago, every other woman was wearing a shingle or a King Tut.
Miss Holden is also quoted by the “China Press” as having given credit to the European ladies of Shanghai for being the leaders of fashion and elegance, rather than their Chinese sisters, but she suggests the Western women get their inspiration from the age old styles of the Orient and adapt them to Occidental ideas.

label: text
text: "In time Chinese girls will discard trousers for European dress," Miss Holden predicts, but it has been obvious even to Hong-kong that China's young womanhood has adopted the skirt for years and that the trousers have almost entirely lost favour with the younger set.

label: text
text: To Shanghai, however, belongs the honour of having set the lead in Chinese fashions—at least since the Revolution. The non-observant should, at the next opportunity, study the styles displayed by the smart Chinese ladies of Hongkong. Watch for the rather full, ankle-length skirt

label: text
text: adopted from Shanghai a season, or two ago—the close fitting jacket with graceful waist lines and smooth, round corners, the very smart colours, the simple yet attractive trimmings of every shade—all these were copied one by one from Shanghai, and even, too, the entirely Western, high-heel shoe with multi-straps for adornment.

label: text
text: Hongkong should certainly see to it that it holds its own in fashion, even if there is no annual interport contest in this line.

label: text
text: An armed robbery is reported to have occurred yesterday afternoon at a house in Shanghai Street occupied by a married woman. The report states that two men entered the house and seized the complainant by the throat whilst she was asleep. They stole from her person jewellery valued at $80. The woman was then gagged and bound and one of the robbers pointed a revolver at her with threats to obtain information to where she kept her money and other valuables. Filling in this the robbers left the house and escaped.
